title: Module 3 · Lesson 2 — LLM-as-a-judge: power and pitfalls

lines: Module Three, Lesson Two: LLM as a judge.
It's powerful, as long as you know how it fails.

say.0: Module Three, Lesson Two: L L M as a judge.

lines: Picture a news app whose agent writes ten thousand summaries a day.
Good summaries never match word for word, and no editor can read them all.
So the team has another model grade every summary.
That's LLM as a judge: a scorer that scales.

say.1: That's L L M as a judge: a scorer that scales.

lines: Judges shine where quality is real but can't be string-matched.
Think summary quality, tone, helpfulness, or groundedness in a source.
But if a deterministic check exists, use code instead.
Schemas, numbers, passing tests, or the right tool call are cheaper, faster, and unbiased in code.
Next, learn to name the judge's four biases.
Position bias favors the first answer, so score both orders and average.
In the news app, the top-rated summaries were simply the longest.
That's verbosity bias, fixed with a rubric that rewards information density.
The same model family also wrote and judged, inflating every score.
That's self-preference, so use a judge from a different family.
Score compression clusters everything at seven or eight out of ten.
Pairwise comparison or a short discrete rubric spreads the scores out.
Now, design a judge that holds up.
Ask which of two answers is better, and anchor the rubric with examples of a one, a three, and a five.
Make the judge write its reasoning before its score.
Scoring first turns the reasoning into an after-the-fact excuse.
Then calibrate on one to two hundred expert-labeled cases, measuring agreement with Cohen's kappa.
A judge agreeing only sixty percent of the time is measuring something else.
Finally, pin the judge's version like any other dependency.
A silent provider upgrade would change your whole metric history.
NVIDIA's NeMo Evaluator runs benchmarks, custom datasets, and judges as comparable scored runs.
After a fine-tune, it answers: did the new model beat the incumbent?

say.0: En-vidia's Neemo Evaluator runs benchmarks, custom datasets, and judges as comparable scored runs.

lines: Exam tip: if one option is a code check instead of a judge, pick the code.
And suspiciously high scores point to self-preference; read on for all four biases.
